career_switcher-01-office-to-office.q1: I had a junior BI analyst interview at a fintech firm in Singapore. It was a two‑round process: first a 30‑minute phone screen with HR, then a 45‑minute on‑site with the analytics team. The on‑site was a panel of two senior analysts and a manager.
career_switcher-01-office-to-office.q2: I spent about four hours preparing. I skimmed the job description, read a few LinkedIn posts on BI roles, and watched a couple of YouTube videos on SQL basics. I asked my sister to ask me some behavioural questions. Nothing cost money.
career_switcher-01-office-to-office.q3: The hardest part was the SQL question where they asked me to write a query to find the top three customers by revenue. I didn't have time to practice advanced joins, so I got stuck and had to guess. That moment made me realise my gaps.
career_switcher-01-office-to-office.q4: I was surprised that the panel asked me to walk through a recent project I did in my admin role, even though it was unrelated to data. They wanted to see how I could translate my organisational skills into analytics.
career_switcher-01-office-to-office.q5: I wish I had a quick reference sheet of common SQL patterns and a short mock interview with a friend who knows data. My family commitments and the fact that I had already spent on a bootcamp stopped me from investing more time.
career_switcher-01-office-to-office.q6: Yes, I tried a free AI mock interview app once. It asked me questions and gave instant feedback, but I found the suggestions generic and stopped after a few rounds because it felt too scripted.
career_switcher-01-office-to-office.q7: I’m a bit uneasy about my answers being recorded. I worry about privacy and where the data is stored, so I prefer tools that let me delete the recordings after the session.
career_switcher-01-office-to-office.q8: I think it would be useful if the tool could read the job posting and my profile, but I’m not sure it would help me much. I’d still need to decide what to practise – the tool might give me a generic list of questions that are common in BI interviews, but I’m worried it could push me to rehearse the wrong things. I’d prefer a checklist that I can tick off myself rather than a tool telling me what to do. Also, I’m not 100% comfortable letting a tool analyse my profile because of privacy concerns. So I’d use it only if it’s very clear how it’s using my data and if it lets me delete everything after I’m done.
career_switcher-01-office-to-office.q9: The question about the project I did in my admin role was a bit vague – they didn’t specify what aspects of the project they wanted to hear about, so I had to guess what they were looking for. Also, when they asked me to walk through the SQL query, they didn’t say if they wanted a full solution or just the thought process, which made me feel like I was missing the point. I didn’t feel any question was nudging me toward a specific answer, but the lack of clarity made me uncertain about how to answer.
career_switcher-01-office-to-office.q8n: I would quickly review a cheat sheet of SQL patterns, practise a couple of basic joins, and jot down a short story about my admin project that shows data thinking. I’d also ask a friend to run a 5‑minute mock Q&A on behavioural questions, focusing on how I translate scheduling skills to data insights. If I had a tool that let me delete the recordings, I’d use it for a quick run‑through of the interview format.

career_switcher-02-nonoffice-to-office.q1: I had an interview for HR associate at a mid‑size tech firm last month. It was two rounds – first a phone screen with HR, then a video call with the HR manager and a hiring manager. All were one‑on‑one, no panel.
career_switcher-02-nonoffice-to-office.q2: I spent about an hour looking up the company’s website and reading the job description again. I asked my sister, who works in HR, to give me a quick run‑through of typical questions. Nothing paid, just my own time.
career_switcher-02-nonoffice-to-office.q3: The hardest part was a question about handling a conflict between two team members. I wasn’t ready with a concrete example, so I improvised and said I’d just let them talk. I felt the interviewer was looking for a structured approach.
career_switcher-02-nonoffice-to-office.q4: I expected a phone call first, but the first round was a video call. I didn’t have a good webcam setup, so it was a bit awkward.
career_switcher-02-nonoffice-to-office.q5: I wish I had a better example of a people‑management metric from my retail days. I was too busy finishing a shift at the store to prepare more, so I didn’t spend extra time on STAR stories.
career_switcher-02-nonoffice-to-office.q6: I tried an online mock interview app once. It was clunky and the questions felt generic. I stopped because it was too time‑consuming and not really helpful.
career_switcher-02-nonoffice-to-office.q7: I’m not comfortable with my voice or video being recorded. I worry about where the data goes and who can see it. I’d rather just have a quick feedback session instead of a full recording.
career_switcher-02-nonoffice-to-office.q8: I don’t think so. I’ve never used a tool that maps a job posting to my profile. It feels too much like a magic box that might not understand my retail background. I’d rather stick to what I know and just use the company site and my sister’s help. Plus I’m worried about data privacy on those platforms.
career_switcher-02-nonoffice-to-office.q9: The question about handling conflict felt a bit vague. It didn’t say whether they wanted a formal mediation approach or just a quick fix. I felt the interviewer was nudging me to say I’d just let them talk, which is not how they expect an HR pro to respond. That question was the only one that was unclear to me.
career_switcher-02-nonoffice-to-office.q8n: I’d grab the job spec again, jot down a few quick STAR points from my shift scheduling wins, and set up a decent webcam with good lighting. I’d practice answering the conflict question with a clear steps outline. I’d want help only with a quick run‑through of that answer, nothing fancy.

low_wage_worker-01-cafe-jan23.q1: I had a 30‑minute walk‑in interview at a local coffee shop for a barista part‑time role. It was just me and the manager, no panel. The whole thing was on the spot, no prior notice.
low_wage_worker-01-cafe-jan23.q2: I just googled “barista interview questions” for about 15 mins. Watched a couple of short TikTok clips from a friend who worked there. No money spent, just my phone. I didn’t really get help from anyone else.
low_wage_worker-01-cafe-jan23.q3: The hardest part was when they asked about how to make a latte with a frother. I didn’t know the steps, so I fumbled and said I’d learn. That moment felt like a total fail.
low_wage_worker-01-cafe-jan23.q4: I was surprised that the interview was so quick and informal. I expected a 30‑minute chat, but it was over in like 10 mins. No formal thank‑you email, just a quick “thanks” in person.
low_wage_worker-01-cafe-jan23.q5: I wish I had a proper résumé or a thank‑you email template. I was too busy delivering food and didn’t have time to draft anything. Also, I didn’t have a clear idea of what to highlight from my diploma.
low_wage_worker-01-cafe-jan23.q6: No, I never used an AI mock interview. I heard about it but thought it’s too expensive and not really useful for a simple barista role.
low_wage_worker-01-cafe-jan23.q7: I’m a bit uneasy about recording my voice or video. I worry where it will be stored and if it can be shared. I’d rather keep it offline if possible.
low_wage_worker-01-cafe-jan23.q8: I think I might try that if it’s free, but I’m not sure. If the tool can show me what the coffee shop wants and I can see my own profile fit, maybe I’ll give it a go. But I don’t want to waste time or money on something I don’t know if it helps. Also, I’m not super tech‑savvy, so I worry about the interface. If it’s simple and shows me clear tips, I’ll try, otherwise I’ll skip.
low_wage_worker-01-cafe-jan23.q9: The question about making a latte with a frother was a bit vague. I didn’t know if they wanted the steps or if they were testing my knowledge. Also, when they asked if I could work weekends, I wasn’t sure if they were just checking availability or if they wanted me to say yes right away. Those felt like nudges to give a quick answer.
low_wage_worker-01-cafe-jan23.q8n: If tomorrow got another interview, I’d just skim some quick barista tips on TikTok, maybe ask a friend who’s been there for a quick demo. I’d also try to write a short thank‑you note on my phone, but I’m not sure how to phrase it formally. Basically, I want a quick guide on what skills to flaunt and a simple thank‑you template that feels natural, not too fancy.

low_wage_worker-02-warehouse-lee.q1: I had a trial shift interview for a loader job at a logistics centre. One person, the manager, asked me a few questions after I did the shift. No panel, just one round. It was a quick chat in the break room.
low_wage_worker-02-warehouse-lee.q2: I just asked my friend who works there to tell me what to do. I did not read any articles. I did not use any videos or AI. I did not spend much time. Nothing cost money. I just came early and wore clean clothes.
low_wage_worker-02-warehouse-lee.q3: The hardest part was when he asked me about safety rules. I was not ready. He said, 'Do you know how to lift heavy boxes safely?' I said, 'Yes, I lift boxes all day.' He looked at me and said, 'But do you know the correct way to lift?' I felt stuck. That was the moment.
low_wage_worker-02-warehouse-lee.q4: I did not expect that he would ask about safety. I thought it would just be a quick chat. I was surprised that he asked about lifting technique. I didn't expect a question about a certification. It was a surprise.
low_wage_worker-02-warehouse-lee.q5: I would have liked to know more about the safety certification. I did not have time because I had to go to work. I also did not have a computer or internet to read. I was busy with my shift. I could not prepare more because of the time. I only had a few minutes. I did not have a phone with internet. I could not look up anything. I was busy. I did not have time. I was tired. I did not have a laptop. I was stuck. I did not have a way to practice. I could not do more. I had to go home. I was tired. I did not have time.
low_wage_worker-02-warehouse-lee.q6: I have never used an AI mock interview. I do not know what it is. I have never tried it. I do not use any practice tools. I only use what my friend says. I do not use AI. I do not use any mock interview. I do not have any. I have not used it. I have never tried. I do not know. I did not use it.
low_wage_worker-02-warehouse-lee.q7: I do not know how it would feel. I have not tried it. I am not comfortable with recording. I would not want my voice recorded. I do not know where it would be stored. I am not sure. I would not want it stored. I do not know. I do not know. I would not want it.
low_wage_worker-02-warehouse-lee.q8: No, I don't want to use a tool. I don't know what it does. I think it is for smart jobs. I work hard, need steady job, not fancy software.
low_wage_worker-02-warehouse-lee.q9: The safety question was unclear. I didn't know the right answer. The manager asked about how to lift boxes safely. I was not ready. It felt like he wanted a specific answer.
low_wage_worker-02-warehouse-lee.q8n: I would go home, ask my friend to show me the right way to lift boxes, and maybe practice with a friend. I want help to know the exact safety steps and maybe a quick list of questions the manager might ask. I would also like a simple guide on what to say when they ask about certifications.

foreign_professional-01-german-tech.q1: The last interview was for a Senior Backend Engineer at a Singapore fintech. It was a three‑round process: first a phone screen with HR, second a technical coding test via a shared Google Doc, and third a video call with two senior engineers. The video call was a panel, but each spoke in turn.
foreign_professional-01-german-tech.q2: I spent about five hours. I reviewed the company’s technical blog, re‑wrote my own project summaries, and ran through a few coding problems on LeetCode. I did not use any paid services; just my laptop and a free online IDE. No friends or family were involved.
foreign_professional-01-german-tech.q3: The hardest part was the system design question. I had never been asked to design a distributed ledger system in a live interview. During the question, I struggled to explain how I would handle eventual consistency, and I paused for a full minute before responding.
foreign_professional-01-german-tech.q4: The panel format surprised me because the two engineers were both senior but had different styles; one was very formal, the other used a lot of local slang. I had expected a single interviewer.
foreign_professional-01-german-tech.q5: I would have liked a more detailed interview guide from the recruiter. My time was limited by a current project deadline, so I couldn’t rehearse system design scenarios as much as I wanted.
foreign_professional-01-german-tech.q6: I have not used an AI mock interview tool. I prefer human‑reviewed resources and feel AI might give me generic answers.
foreign_professional-01-german-tech.q7: I am uncomfortable with any tool that records my voice or video. I worry about where the data is stored and how it might be accessed by third parties.
foreign_professional-01-german-tech.q8: I would not practise inside such a tool. Even if it knew the job posting and my profile, the risk of receiving generic, AI‑generated responses outweighs any potential benefit. I prefer to rely on official documentation, technical blogs, and hands‑on coding. A tool that tailors content to my profile might also reinforce my distrust of AI, as it could produce answers that feel scripted rather than authentic. Moreover, the tool’s data handling policies are unclear, and I am uncomfortable with any system that records or stores my personal information. Therefore, I would avoid it.
foreign_professional-01-german-tech.q9: During the system design question, the interviewer asked me to design a distributed ledger system. While the question itself was clear, the interviewer’s follow‑up about handling eventual consistency felt like a nudge toward a specific architectural pattern. Additionally, when the second senior engineer used local slang to ask about my experience with microservices, the phrasing was ambiguous, and I was unsure whether he was probing for depth or simply checking for cultural fit. These moments left me slightly uncertain about the exact expectations.
foreign_professional-01-german-tech.q8n: I would quickly review the company’s recent technical posts and re‑examine my own project summaries, then run a short LeetCode warm‑up for 30 minutes. I’d also outline a concise system‑design framework for distributed ledgers, focusing on consistency and fault tolerance. If I had help, it would be a clear, concise interview guide from the recruiter, not an AI tool.

job_seeker-01-senior-phone.q1: I had one interview, for a security guard job. It was just one round, face‑to‑face, one man from the company. He asked a few questions and then left.
job_seeker-01-senior-phone.q2: I asked my neighbour to help me call the office and confirm the time. I spent about 20 minutes on the phone, no money spent. I didn’t use any videos or anything, just a quick chat with him.
job_seeker-01-senior-phone.q3: The hardest part was when he asked about my computer skills. I didn’t know how to answer because I don’t use a computer much. I said I could learn, but I felt nervous.
job_seeker-01-senior-phone.q4: I expected a longer interview, but it was short. That surprised me a bit, but it was fine.
job_seeker-01-senior-phone.q5: I wish I had a printed list of common questions. I didn’t have time to ask anyone else because I was busy with my health. That stopped me from preparing more.
job_seeker-01-senior-phone.q6: No, I have never used an AI mock interview. I don’t think it would help me, and I’m not comfortable with that kind of thing.
job_seeker-01-senior-phone.q7: I would not like to be recorded. I don’t know where the voice would be stored and it makes me uneasy.
job_seeker-01-senior-phone.q8: I think it would be hard. I don’t use computers much, and I don’t like to be in a room with a screen that keeps talking. I’d rather have a paper list or a neighbour help me. If the tool could print the questions for me, maybe I could try it, but I’m not sure I would trust it.
job_seeker-01-senior-phone.q9: The only unclear one was when he asked about my computer skills. I didn’t know what he meant by that, and I felt pushed to say I could learn. I didn’t get a clear idea of what level he was expecting.
job_seeker-01-senior-phone.q8n: I would call my neighbour again and ask him to help me pick up the interview time and place. I would also ask him to show me how to write a simple note with the questions, so I can read it aloud. I would like him to stay with me during the interview to ask me what to say if I get stuck. I don't want any video or recording, just a friendly chat.

job_seeker-01-no-prep-spontaneity.q1: I got an interview for a marketing coordinator role at a small e‑commerce start‑up. It was just one round, a video call with the HR rep and the creative lead. They asked a few quick questions and then we did a short task to see how I’d handle a social media post.
job_seeker-01-no-prep-spontaneity.q2: I didn’t really prep. I just skimmed the company website for a bit and watched one YouTube video about interview tips. No money spent, just my own time after barista shift. I asked my friend who works in marketing to give me a quick pep talk, but that’s about it.
job_seeker-01-no-prep-spontaneity.q3: The hardest part was when they asked about my experience with analytics tools. I didn’t have any real experience, so I fumbled. I tried to say I’d used Google Analytics once at a gig, but I couldn’t explain how it worked. That was the moment I felt most out of my depth.
job_seeker-01-no-prep-spontaneity.q4: I was surprised that they asked me to create a mock post on the spot. I didn’t expect a creative task during the interview, but it was actually cool to show what I could do on the fly.
job_seeker-01-no-prep-spontaneity.q5: I wish I had done a quick review of the company culture and their recent campaigns. I didn’t have time because my shift was late and I was tired. I also didn’t want to look too rehearsed, so I skipped a proper prep checklist.
job_seeker-01-no-prep-spontaneity.q6: I tried an AI mock interview app once, but it felt too scripted. I stopped after a couple of questions because it was too robotic and I didn’t feel like myself.
job_seeker-01-no-prep-spontaneity.q7: I’m not comfortable with my answers being recorded or stored. I’d rather keep my conversation private and not have my voice in some database. It just feels too formal and not like me.
job_seeker-01-no-prep-spontaneity.q8: I dun think I wanna use that kind of tool, lah. I feel it’ll just make my answers all copy‑paste and not show my real vibe. Plus, if it reads my profile and job post, it might try to push me into some template answers that sound too rehearsed, which I don’t like. I just wanna keep it natural, even if it means I look a bit raw. Also, I’m not sure I trust it with my personal info, you know?
job_seeker-01-no-prep-spontaneity.q9: The analytics question was kinda weird, because I didn’t really do any analytics work before. They just asked me if I had used any tools, and I was like, “yeah, Google Analytics once.” That felt like they were nudging me to say I had experience when I didn’t. Also the task to make a mock post on the spot was a bit surprising, but I kinda liked it. The rest were pretty clear, just basic stuff.
job_seeker-01-no-prep-spontaneity.q8n: Next one, I’d just grab the company’s LinkedIn and skim their posts, maybe ask my barista buddy for a quick chat about what they’re into. I’d also try to find a free Canva template and practice whipping up a post in 5 mins, so I’m not all nervous. I could use a quick rundown on what analytics tools look like, but I’d keep it short and real.

early_career-01-ai‑prep‑grad.q1: Last week, I had a 90‑minute technical screen for a junior dev role at a fintech startup. It was a one‑on‑one over Teams, followed by a coding challenge in an online IDE. The panel was just the hiring manager and a senior engineer.
early_career-01-ai‑prep‑grad.q2: I spent about 4 hours total: 1 hour on the company website, 1 hour on LeetCode for data‑structures, 1 hour with the AI assistant summarising interview questions, and 1 hour rehearsing answers. I paid nothing; the AI was free and the mock platform was built into the job portal.
early_career-01-ai‑prep‑grad.q3: The hardest part was a system‑design question on building a payment gateway. I hadn’t prepared for scaling concerns, so I froze for 30 seconds and then improvised. That moment felt like a gap in my knowledge.
early_career-01-ai‑prep‑grad.q4: I expected a panel interview, but it was just two people. The senior engineer asked a behavioral question about failure, which I wasn’t ready for in that depth.
early_career-01-ai‑prep‑grad.q5: I wish I had a quick run‑through of the company’s recent product releases to tailor my answers. Time pressure from the next interview slot stopped me from digging deeper.
early_career-01-ai‑prep‑grad.q6: Yes, I used an AI mock interview that gave instant feedback on my answers. I kept going until the AI flagged a few weak points, but then I stopped because I felt the script was becoming too rehearsed.
early_career-01-ai‑prep‑grad.q7: I’m fine with voice recording if it helps spot filler words, but I’d prefer the data to stay local. I’m wary of cloud storage and would avoid any platform that didn’t clearly state where my data goes.
early_career-01-ai‑prep‑grad.q8: Yeah, I'd try it. A tool that ingests the posting and my CV can auto‑highlight gaps like payment‑gateway scaling or fintech APIs. It saves time over manual research and gives me targeted prompts. The only hitch is that it might push me to over‑script answers, so I'd keep a sanity check by re‑phrasing in my own words after the AI gives a draft.
early_career-01-ai‑prep‑grad.q9: The senior engineer’s question about failure was oddly vague: "Tell me about a time you failed and what you learned." It felt like he wanted a specific anecdote rather than a generic answer. I sensed he was nudging me to showcase resilience, but the wording left me guessing if he wanted a project failure or a personal slip.
early_career-01-ai‑prep‑grad.q8n: I’d skim the fintech’s recent blog posts for product updates, then run a 30‑min LeetCode session on concurrency problems, and do a quick AI‑run mock to flag any filler words. I’d also ask the AI to generate a few behavioral prompts that dig into failure scenarios so I don’t feel stuck. Finally, I’d want instant feedback on my code walk‑throughs to keep the answers crisp.
